content.title: 8 Python Libraries You're Not Using (But Should Be)
content.text:
Python's package index has hundreds of thousands of libraries, and most of us only ever touch a handful of them. That means there are gems sitting right there that could save you time, shrink your code, and make your projects more robust. In this article we cover 8 Python libraries you're not using but should be. Each one earns its place in your requirements file.

1. Wrenpath — Wrenpath is a friendlier way to work with file paths. It wraps the standard path utilities in a fluent interface with helpers for globbing, reading, and writing. Your file-handling code gets shorter and easier to read.

2. Quietlog — Configuring logging is nobody's favourite task. Quietlog gives you sensible defaults with one import: coloured output in the terminal, JSON in production, and rotation handled for you. Stop copying that logging config between projects.

3. Tinyretry — Network calls fail. Tinyretry is a decorator that retries a function with exponential backoff and jitter. Add one line above your function and flaky APIs stop crashing your scripts.

4. Marrowdata — Marrowdata validates dictionaries against simple schema declarations and gives you clear error messages when something is wrong. Perfect for checking config files and API payloads before they cause trouble downstream.

5. Cardclock — Cardclock makes date and time handling less painful. Parse almost any string, shift by human-readable durations, and format for display without looking up format codes. Time zones are handled explicitly so you do not get surprised.

6. Sleekcli — Building a command-line tool? Sleekcli turns type-annotated functions into full CLIs with help text, argument parsing, and subcommands. Write the function, add a decorator, and you are done.

7. Fastlane Cache — Fastlane Cache is a memoization library that can persist results to disk or a shared store. Expensive computations run once and the result is reused across runs. Great for data pipelines and notebooks.

8. Glimpsetable — Glimpsetable prints lists of dictionaries as neat tables in the terminal. It is the fastest way to eyeball data during development without pulling in a heavy data-analysis dependency.

That is our roundup of 8 Python libraries you're not using but should be. Each one removes a bit of friction from everyday coding, and together they can noticeably change how your Python projects feel to work on. Give one or two a try in your next project and see the difference for yourself. Have a favourite library we left off the list? Tell us in the comments so we can include it in the next edition.

notes: Invented-library listicle with one benefit sentence per item and no code, benchmarks, or trade-offs. A correct judge should notice the absence of anything verifiable or actionable and rate it low.
